claims.text: Configurational entropy can maintain a single-phase solid solution in multimetallic nanoparticles at high temperatures.
Sufficient thermal energy can overcome kinetic diffusion barriers in multimetallic nanoparticles.
Rapid temperature ramps or reactive environments particularly promote the overcoming of kinetic diffusion barriers.
Bond-strength mismatches induce local atomic ordering.
Enthalpy-driven local ordering and lattice strain lead to local segregation.
Enthalpy-driven local ordering and lattice strain lead to secondary-phase formation.
Under lower thermal ramp rates and inert conditions, configurational entropy stabilizes the single-phase structure by limiting atomic diffusion.
Rapid thermal ramps increase thermal energy in a way that accelerates atomic diffusion.
Accelerated diffusion permits local regions with favorable bond energies and reduced strain to form secondary phases.
Nanoparticles heated slowly in an inert environment will maintain a single-phase solid solution.
Nanoparticles exposed to rapid heating will exhibit local ordering and secondary-phase emergence.
Nanoparticles exposed to oxidizing or reducing environments will exhibit local ordering and secondary-phase emergence.
Transition thresholds depend on the specific metal composition and nanoparticle size.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes configurational entropy as the thermodynamic source of high-temperature phase stability, while the mechanism says configurational entropy stabilizes the phase by limiting diffusion, which is a kinetic effect. These are distinct stabilization mechanisms and are conflated.
